chapters.summary: Council Member Shekar Krishnan opens the hearing, identifies himself as chair of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations, and thanks Speaker Julie Menin and colleagues for serving. He notes the joint nature of the hearing with Consumer and Worker Protection.
chapters.title: Krishnan calls hearing to order and thanks Speaker and committee

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This hearing is called to order.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Shaker Krishnan, Chair of the Committee on Oversight and Investigations, and I would like to thank Speaker Julie Menon for entrusting me with sharing this crucial committee and my colleagues for serving on the committee and joining us today.

chapters.summary: Krishnan says the hearing will examine the Oversight and Investigations Division's report on flavored e-cigarettes near New York City public schools. He thanks co-chair Harvey Epstein, DCWP representatives, members of the public, and colleagues including Carr, Narcisse, Hanks, and Shulman.
chapters.title: Krishnan states purpose: examining flavored e-cigarette availability near schools

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Today we'll be examining the Oversight and Investigations Division's report on the availability of flavored e-cigarettes or vapes near New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'd like to thank my co-chair and longtime good friend, Councilmember Harvey Epstein, Chair of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection, for co-chairing this hearing with me.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the representatives from the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, members of the public, and my council colleagues who have joined us here today, including Councilmember Carr and Councilmember Narcisse, and Councilmember Hanks is in the building too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The sharp decline.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Oh, and Councilmember Shulman is online as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Krishnan says the decline in youth tobacco smoking was a public health triumph, but e-cigarettes and vapes are undoing decades of progress. He highlights flavored vapes designed to appeal to youth, the 2020 state ban, and studies showing sales fell after the ban.
chapters.title: Krishnan gives public health context on youth vaping and state flavor ban

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The sharp decline in youth tobacco smoking is one of the greatest public health triumphs in recent American history.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But now that battle has entered a second round.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The collapse of tobacco...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Smoking among young people was driven by vigorous regulation, public education, and restrictions on advertising targeting minors.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But the recent spread of e-cigarettes and vapes is undoing decades of progress.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And now the fight against big tobacco has entered a new phase.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Especially concerning are flavored e-cigarettes and vapes that taste like fruits and candy, which are designed and deployed to appeal and market to younger consumers.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Since 2020, New York State has banned the sale of flavored nicotine vapor products, or vapes, to protect our children and youth from these addictive and harmful products.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: At the time the ban was passed, the State Department of Health found that a quarter of New York City high school students used vapes, especially those with sweet and fruit flavors.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Studies found that after the ban was passed, sales of these products that appeal to young and vulnerable consumers fell sharply.

chapters.summary: Krishnan says the Oversight report found many retailers near schools continue selling banned flavored vapes. Investigators found licensed stores selling illegal products and that 100% of unlicensed stores were selling illegal vapes.
chapters.title: Krishnan summarizes report findings on illegal vape sales near schools

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But the work is not done, and retailers have flouted the law.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As the oversight and investigation division found in the report we are reviewing today, many retailers located close to New York City schools continue to sell

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: banned or illegal flavored e-cigarettes or vapes, posing a major risk to the health and well-being of our young New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I really want to thank our Oversight and Investigation Division for their excellent work on this report.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Once again, through meticulous investigation, analysis, and a thoughtful report that really uncovers and highlights an issue that otherwise we wouldn't know as much about.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The report raises serious questions about the enforcement of New York's ban on the sale of flavored vape products.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Our investigators found that even licensed stores sell these illegal products despite the risk they pose to their ability to continue operating lawfully if caught.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The investigators also found unlicensed stores brazenly selling flavored vapes despite not being licensed to sell any tobacco or nicotine products at all.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In fact, what the report found was that 100% or every single one of the unlicensed stores, unlicensed to sell vapes, were selling illegal vapes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So not only were they not licensed to sell any kinds of vapes, but they were all selling an illegal category of vapes as well.

chapters.summary: Krishnan questions why retailers flout the law with impunity and notes many already faced enforcement actions. He says none of the caught businesses were sealed by DCWP and suggests current penalties may be too light, requiring laws with real teeth.
chapters.title: Krishnan raises enforcement gaps and need for stronger penalties and sealing

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So today, we ask, why are New York City retailers flouting this law with such impunity?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We seek to understand how our consumer protection and public health agencies are combating the illegal sale of flavored e-cigarettes, especially near our schools.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Many of the stores that our investigators found selling flavored vapes had already been subject to enforcement actions for this conduct.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Which raises the question of whether the current regulations are strong enough to dissuade retailers from offering illegal products, or if they are so light that stores simply consider them a cost of doing business.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: None of the businesses caught selling illegal vape products have been sealed by enforcement agencies like DCWP, and I hope we can find a way to change that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: If businesses feel they can flout the law with only minor consequences, then the council and the state may have to revise these laws to give them real teeth.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: From the ONI committee staff, Nicole Kata, Eric Cohen, Alex Yablon, and Owen Katowski.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And for my staff, Chanel Martinez, Hunter DeVine-Gracia, and Victoria Opperman.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And of course, to everyone in this hearing today who are making it run successfully.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to my co-chair, Councilman Breffstein, for his opening statement.

chapters.title: Epstein describes illegal flavored vapes near schools and report finding

utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Krishnan, and thank you for your leadership on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That's just, you know, since 2019 when the council made flavor of vapes illegal, we've seen a proliferation of these stores across the city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I was just in my district yesterday walking past the school and across the street from there was illegal flavor of vapes with like.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Captain Crunch things in the cereal, in the window, Captain Crunch and other cereal-looking items, all these illegal flavor vapes, all these flavors that we know are attracting just to our young people.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: As Councilmember Christian just discussed, the report found that illegal flavored cigarettes remain widely available here in public schools.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 40% business survey offered prohibited e-flavored cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So many of these in Manhattan and across our city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This is totally unacceptable, and we look forward to this robust conversation with DCWP staff about how we get in front of this.

chapters.title: Epstein compares liquor enforcement and supports Narcisse sealing bill

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, you think about a lot of things that are illegal, but you never see someone who...

utterances.text: doesn't have a liquor license, open up a wine store or a liquor shop, and this stays open.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It just doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: For some reason, you can open, you can have a flavor vape store, and we know it's illegal, and it just remains open year after year after year.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I also look forward to discussing Council Member Narciso's good legislation, 1161, tend to give DCWP additional tools in their toolbox,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: grant you authority to seal premises for e-cigarettes that are found to be repeatedly sold and not licensed.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I really want to thank the staff from Natalie and Sarah from DCWP for all their work to make this happen.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: My team, Jenna and Jackson, to kind of help us get to this day.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And they, you know, oh, and I said, no jackets today, though.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm really disappointed.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I just want to say, you know, I was looking forward to the, you know, we got to bring the jackets back because, you know, it's the look.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It really is.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I thank Councilmember Christian for his leadership and work to bring us to this day today.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.title: Krishnan invites Narcisse; Narcisse describes youth exposure to candy-flavored vapes

utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And now, Councilman Narcisse, if you wanted to do an opening statement on your legislation.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So it is the right time right now to address this conversation, our kids being addicted left and right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if you walk down almost any commercial strip in the city of New York, you will find a shop selling flavored vapes, all the things that I just spoke, cotton candy and all of those.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

chapters.title: Narcisse says fines are cost of business and touts Intro 1167 sealing authority

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They sell products that are banned.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And when they get caught, they pay the fine and keep going.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For some of these jobs, a fine is just a cost of doing business.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They don't care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They pay it and they keep moving.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And through 1167 changes that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That breaks the law.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If you're a good businessman, your store should stay open.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm a businesswoman, a small businesswoman for many years.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.text: These addictive and dangerous flavored products are made to appeal to young people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Our agencies have been asked.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We need to protect small businesses, and that's what I come to the angle to protect folks that are doing a good job in our city.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to thank the speaker, of course, for her partnership on this, and I ask my colleagues, of course, to support this.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's about time to protect our children in New York City, so thank you.

chapters.summary: Carlos Ortiz, DCWP Chief of Staff, introduces himself and colleagues Deputy General Counsel Andrew Schwenk and Associate Commissioner Haley Radiker. He thanks the committee for the opportunity to testify.
chapters.title: Ortiz introduces himself and DCWP colleagues

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Epstein, Chair Krishnan, and Council Member Narcisse, and members of the committee on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My name is Carlos Ortiz, and I am the Chief of Staff of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I am joined by our Deputy General Counsel, Andrew Schwenk, and Associate Commissioner of Intergovernmental Affairs, Haley Radiker.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify before the committee on this topic and legislation.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP enforces state and city laws on tobacco and e-cigarette sales, including flavor prohibitions, age restrictions, signage, and display rules. He describes the Field Enforcement Division's 84 staff, education team, inspection bureau, and undercover youth purchase unit.
chapters.title: Ortiz outlines DCWP tobacco and e-cigarette enforcement responsibilities and units

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCAP is tasked with enforcing New York State and New York City laws related to the sale of tobacco and electronic cigarettes, as well as license requirements for retailers that sell tobacco and electronic cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This includes prohibitions against certain flavored products, sales to minors, package size requirements, signage requirements, advertisement and display prohibitions, and more.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCAP's Field Enforcement Division has a total of 84 active staff, operating both in the field and as support.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There are three separate units that work with tobacco and electronic cigarette retailers, providing business education, conducting comprehensive compliance inspections, and

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: coordinating undercover youth purchase attempts.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Our VIP visiting inspector program, a business education team, provides education to businesses, working to ensure retailers are aware of the regulations and in compliance with our laws.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Our field enforcement bureau conducts patrol inspections and complaint-based inspections, including inspections at businesses believed to be engaged in tobacco or e-cigarette activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Lastly, our dedicated tobacco unit works undercover with underage youth to make purchase attempts.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And together with our agency's attorneys, these teams aggressively enforce and adjudicate violations against recidivist businesses that believe they are above the law.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP conducted nearly 12,000 tobacco inspections and 10,300 e-cigarette inspections in 2026. This led to nearly 4,000 summonses, $3.6 million in penalties, and 240 padlocked non-compliant tobacco retailers since 2023.
chapters.title: Ortiz presents 2026 enforcement statistics and padlock numbers

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Our strategic field enforcement has improved our efforts over the last several years and focuses inspections on businesses with repeat violation history and complaints from the community.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thus far in 2026, our enforcement team has conducted close to 12,000 tobacco inspections and 10,300 e-cigarette inspections.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This work has led to nearly 4,000 summonses and the collection of $3.6 million in penalties in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we've been able to padlock 240 non-compliant tobacco retailers since 2023.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Regulating this industry and enforcing against bad actors has been and will continue to be a core part of our work at DCVP, and we look forward to working with the Council on these efforts.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP sends six undercover youth teams daily to enforce age restrictions. He notes special requirements for businesses within 500 feet of schools, including prohibitions on displaying tobacco paraphernalia or advertisements.
chapters.title: Ortiz details youth purchase attempts and school-proximity rules

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCUP's tobacco unit regularly and repeatedly conducts undercover youth purchase attempts, typically sending out six teams daily to enforce the age restriction on purchases of e-cigarette products.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This includes enforcing specific requirements for businesses located within 500 feet of a school, including prohibitions displaying tobacco, any cigarette paraphernalia, or advertisements, as well as age restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We are committed to protecting youth from illegal underage sales and to protecting the regulated market from illegally operating stores.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we encourage community members to file a complaint directly with our agency.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We would like to thank the council for their work on their report and recommendations to address the issue of flavored e-cigarettes in New York City schools.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This report outlined many of the issues that we are seeing in the industry, and we applaud the efforts taken to bring attention to this issue.

chapters.summary: Ortiz thanks the Council for its report and says DCWP supports its recommendations. He advocates for local legislation requiring disclosure of LLC ownership, saying bad actors hide behind shell LLCs to evade enforcement and penalties.
chapters.title: Ortiz supports report recommendations and LLC transparency

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We are supportive of the recommendations laid out and are actively working with the health department to investigate clear, flavored vapes, conducting proactive inspections of tobacco and e-cigarette.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: retailers in new schools, and collaborating with our sister agencies on youth-facing public health messaging.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In addition to these recommendations, DCP also advocates for pursuing local legislation to create transparency amongst this and other industries by requiring the disclosure of ownership of limited liability companies in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Many of the worst offenders that we see in this industry are hiding behind these LLCs to evade enforcement and the collection of penalties owed to the city.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Bad actors can continue operating by simply incorporating a new LLC and continue to operate under the same ownership.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We appreciate the Council's proposals and look forward to a whole government approach to tackling this issue.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP fully supports Intro 1167, which would grant authority to seal e-cigarette retailers for repeat unlicensed, flavored vape, or underage sale violations. He notes DCWP has used similar tobacco sealing authority to seal 240 recidivist retailers since 2023.
chapters.title: Ortiz supports Intro 1167 sealing authority and cites 240 sealed retailers

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: To arrange today's legislation, Instruction 1167 would grant DCP the authority to seal electronic cigarette retailers for repeat unlicensed flavored e-cigarette or underage sale violations.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCP fully supports this legislation, which would align our authority with the existing ability the agency has to padlock recidivist tobacco retail businesses.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Our current authority only allows us to seal a tobacco retailer dealer until it pays outstanding penalties and enters a consent order to ensure compliance with license requirements and other laws.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And as I mentioned earlier, since 2023, we have used this authority to seal 240 recidivist tobacco retailers for repeated violations of the law.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This legislation would strengthen our enforcement ability and allow us to better address illegal e-cigarette sales across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we look forward to working with the council to pass this bill and being closing down these problematic businesses that are plaguing our community.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify before committee stay on the legislation.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We look forward to working with you all to strengthen our enforcement efforts and abilities.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I welcome any questions you may have for discussion.

chapters.title: Krishnan asks why illegal vapes outpace enforcement; Ortiz cites resources and LLCs

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your agency's work, too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we are actively implementing the historic pledge that the Mayor has given to us in terms of amplifying the resources the agency has.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In terms of enforcement, I think...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You know, I think we are trying to always think creatively about how we can best dedicate our resources.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Even looking through this report, I think there are things that we can do, you know, targeting retailers that are close to schools, for example.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think we can start incorporating that into our enforcement efforts.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think this ability to seal e-cigarette retail dealers now with clear authority, that is a huge tool that we can have now.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I'd also say that it's a challenge constantly in this industry, and other industries too, but in this one in particular with respect to LLCs.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The ability of a business to hide behind a shell LLC and escape liability is something that we are committed to working with the council and the state on as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Because I think that's really a major problem that's coming in this industry too.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks where schools fall in inspection protocols. Ortiz says all inspectors are trained on tobacco and e-cigarette enforcement, and DCWP prioritizes repeat offenders, community complaints, and patrol observations.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks inspection protocols and school priority; Ortiz explains training

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And right now, what are the inspection protocols you have in place?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In other words, where do schools fall on the list?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How are you all looking at retailers that are selling by schools?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, I think we have every single one of our inspectors that joins, no matter what unit they're in, they're trained on tobacco and e-cigarette enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So it is definitely top of mind for our team in terms of our training of inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think right now we prioritize repeat offenders.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We prioritize responsiveness to community complaints.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We are actively looking for these locations when we're on patrol.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think that's been kind of our approach broadly.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But now that we have more of this data and we're able to leverage the report that we've been given by the council, I think we want to use that to reinforce our efforts as well.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks if DCWP inspects all licensed stores yearly. Ortiz says yes, and reports about 12,000 tobacco retail dealer inspections and 10,300 e-cigarette retail dealer inspections so far this year.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about annual licensed inspections and e-cig inspection counts

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And are you all inspecting all licensed stores each year?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We inspect every licensee once a year in this category.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And you may have already said this too, but how many e-cigarette retailer inspections do you all conduct each year?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thus far this year, we've...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thus far this year, we've conducted about 12,000 tobacco retail dealer inspections and 10,300 e-cigarette retail dealer inspections.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I just clarify that some businesses have both licenses, so sometimes we're doing both inspections at that business.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I see.

chapters.summary: Krishnan notes tobacco program inspections fell 32% from FY25 to FY26 and cites MMR language about fewer necessary inspections. Ortiz says the earlier proliferation of unlicensed cannabis shops drove a task force and more inspections, but more work remains.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about 32% inspection decrease; Ortiz explains cannabis shop proliferation

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And tobacco program inspections, which include e-cigarette retailer inspections, decreased by 32% from fiscal year 25 to FY26.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So just in September, in the MMR, it was stated that after three years of increased inspections in response to the proliferation of new smoke shops, quote, many of these businesses were sealed, evicted, or permanently closed.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So fewer tobacco inspections were necessary in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Do you all still see it the same way?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: From July to September of this year, inspections are down compared to the same time frame last year.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And what is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think you've hit the nail on the head, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I mean, I think there's a period of time with the proliferation of particularly unlicensed cannabis shops that were selling e-cigarettes or tobacco products, which just, it was across everywhere in the city.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we, working with our sister agencies like the Sheriff's Office and PD, were actively, we were scaling more inspections.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There was a whole task force dedicated to that work.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Clearly, as this report outlines, though, there's more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think we need to redouble our efforts in terms of where we're targeting our enforcement inspections.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Because I think, as this report has shown, there's still a proliferation of vape activity.

chapters.summary: Krishnan says enforcement may need to refocus on retailers near schools and increase tobacco inspections again. Ortiz says DCWP is open to that approach and that sealing authority will help amplify enforcement.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about redirecting resources to schools; Ortiz open to approach

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think that is an important point because I understand that tobacco inspections may have gone down because places were closed.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But then in the absence of that kind of enforcement, we're seeing it pop up somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so, you know, I know you all, when we've worked together too, even in my district, around the closing of illegal cannabis shops too and how problematic that was.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But I do wonder, even with, you know, the resources you all have, if it is necessary now to redirect or refocus and prioritize schools and retailers by schools in upping tobacco inspections again.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Chair, we're certainly very open to this approach.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think, again, the data from this report, I think, has really shown a light on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And, again, I also want to note as well that I think the ability to seal electronic cigarette stores as well will allow us to amplify enforcement, too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: locations that because of the products they're engaging when we were not able to see them because of our existing authority.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So now this legislation will give us that tool.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether DCWP varies inspection schedules to avoid advance notice, citing undercover findings that licensed shops produced flavored vapes when asked. Ortiz says inspections have no advance notice, are staggered, and include undercover purchases.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about surprise inspections and varying schedules; Ortiz says no advance notice

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One, oh, so one question we had too was, as you all are doing inspections, have you all given thought to varying the schedule so that retailers don't have advance notice?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because one thing we saw in our committee's report and investigations were when our committee staff went in undercover,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: unexpectedly, even if some of the licensed shops did not display flavored vapes, when they asked for them, they would pull them out.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so part of this is with no advance notice, but surprise inspections, there is a possibility of seeing licensed retailers engaging in illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I wonder if you'll give some thought to varying the schedule to avoid any advance notice.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There is no advance notice on our inspections, and I think they are staggered inspections as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it can be evaluated, too, if people are getting advance notice in some way.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Generally, I think if a business is found to be in violation, they will get more than one inspection that year.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We will go back to offenders.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Within that time period as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And when it comes to how we inspect, we do conduct undercover purchases to elicit the product coming out from behind the counter, so to speak.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how often inspectors return to businesses with violations. Ortiz says for underage sales, DCWP will return at least three times in a year.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks frequency of revisits to violators; Ortiz says at least three times

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And then how frequently do inspectors, so if you have a visit,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: that get violations, how frequently are inspectors going back to them to see if they've cured those violations or if they're engaging in more illegal behavior?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, I think give an example of a particular category of underage sales.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We'll go back to an underage sales place at least three times in a year.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay, three times a year at least.

chapters.summary: Krishnan cites the report's finding that unlicensed e-cigarette retailers accrued $1.12 million in penalties but only 0.5% was collected. Ortiz says collections are difficult with fly-by-night operators who open LLCs, sell until caught, and disappear.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about $1.12M penalties and 0.5% collection; Ortiz explains fly-by-night LLCs

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So now I want to get to the main issue, which I think this report really revealed to me too, which is around enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I've always said too, as a former lawyer, the laws are not worth more than the paper they're written on if they're not enforced in reality, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And my concern is, our concern is that a lot of these shops, licensed and unlicensed, just see the cost of breaking the laws across doing business without the enforcement behind it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so one striking statistic that our excellent staff had uncovered was that in serving unlicensed e-cigarette retailers, they accounted for 1.12 million in reported penalties.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In other words, the violations put on them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Accrued to about $1.12 million, but the payment rate was just 0.5%.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So over a million outstanding, which would be a great vehicle to raise funds for the agency too, as I tell HPD as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But only 0.5% have actually been collected.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Are you all aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What is the reason for such a stark rate and discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because on the license side, there was still a big gap there too, and that should be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But the unlicensed was remarkable.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, practically none of the million dollars of fines have been collected.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Did that stand out?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You, were you all aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And what are the practices in place now to help get those fines that are owed?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think collections, we have processes in place for collections, and we collaborate with the law department, both for licensed and unlicensed actors, to collect monies.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Obviously, there's always room for improvement, and we are even working with our sister agencies for better communication channels along those ends.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think the unlicensed side of it, to answer your question directly,

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it has to deal with, in many cases, fly-by-night operators, folks that are not trying to be a part of our marketplace in a regulated way, in a way that's responsible to the public.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And they're literally standing up a business behind an LLC, and then they'll sell until they're caught, and then suddenly they go away.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And you might even see a business there again, but it's a new LLC.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And the way the laws are designed for a notice and opportunity to be heard, we have to enter into a process of violations and adjudications each time.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Now, I would say that Andy's team has done an amazing work in being able to look at those transactions and ensure that actually we can uncover at times through research of it being the same entity, and that helps us keep skin in the game for that entity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Work on collections and ceilings, for example.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And then I think on the other part of besides LLC, I think the ceiling thing is important too, because that will allow us to

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: basically hold the location under padlock, and that will lead to businesses wanting to pay those violations to

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Get that padlock off.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I can maybe throw it over to Andy.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: He can describe a little bit of how our collections are better in the tobacco space compared to the e-cigarette space because of that.

chapters.summary: Schwenk says sealing is a valuable tool and DCWP has collected over $230,000 this fiscal year from targeted sealings. He says sealing also engages landlords about their responsibility to address illegal conduct on their properties, and Ortiz adds $3.8 million collected from 240 sealed tobacco retailers since 2023.
chapters.title: Schwenk explains sealing authority, landlord engagement, and collections

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's all exactly right, Carlos.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, I think what's important here is I think, you know, the oversight committee's report is accurate.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, collections against unlicensed businesses is difficult.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We have known that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We are constantly looking for ways to try to improve that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think sealing as a tool is incredibly helpful.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, just in this fiscal year so far, we've collected over 230,000 from businesses that we've targeted for sealings under our tobacco sealing authority.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: So it's an incredibly valuable tool.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And a downstream effect of that sealing authority that we do use is engaging landlords and property owners as well.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so that can be incredibly effective to get in touch with landlords and property owners and say, you have a responsibility under the administrative code to address illegal conduct at property that you lease out to these fly-by-night operators.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And that has been helpful for engagement on particularly bad actors, repeat actors.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so we think those two things working in combination can be incredibly helpful.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I think that we are always open to new avenues to kind of try to increase our collections across the.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And just to put a data point on this, Chair, since 2023, I mentioned 240 tobacco retailers sealed.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But that also resulted in $3.8 million in collected penalties.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's because they need to pay the penalties before we take the penalties.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: the padlock off.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I just want to reinforce that point as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And that's why the councilman's legislation is so critical.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether LLC evasion is the largest obstacle to collecting fines. Schwenk describes DCWP's collection process, working with the Law Department, and scrutinizing corporate documents and lease history when a new LLC appears at a sealed location.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks biggest obstacle and LLC fine collection process; Schwenk explains sham transactions

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And before we continue, I want to say we've been joined by Councilmember Lee and Councilmember Brewer as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Just going to that point, and we want to talk about LLCs in a minute too, because I think that's a big part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I think the tools that we're going to pass now will be helpful for you all too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What's been the biggest obstacle up till now?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So 1.1 million owed, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These are violations on the businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Let's say they do close the LLC.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, is the LLC issue the largest reason why?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because at some level, I also want to understand, you know, if they're deliberately evading paying fines by...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Closing an LLC and opening a new one, there must be some tools now to go after them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is it a lack of prioritization across agencies?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because I know you have to work together.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So just walk me through the process a bit of one retailer accrues substantial penalties.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Where is that decision made whether to seek fine collection or not?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a great question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think, you know, to start with the collections process, you know, we work on collections internally at DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And if unsuccessful, we also work with the law department and their collections team there, who also has contracts with debt collectors to try to collect on that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: But I think in terms of, you know, targeting particular locations,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: When we have a, I think, fly-by-night LLC that has popped up, what we do see is we'll go back for, we'll identify violations, we'll adjudicate those violations at oath.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, business is found in violation.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That results in a follow-up inspection from our team, knowing that we need to go back and check on compliance at this location.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And often we'll find a new LLC operating at the same location.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And...

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That's a real problem.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: It's a real difficulty.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we do have the best sort of approach forward to address that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: But what we do do is when we do use our sealing authority, we will dig into those transactions.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: So if we show up to a location to seal a business that has a history of violations, and if we find there's a new LLC operating or claiming to be operating there, we will scrutinize the transaction.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We demand corporate documents.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We demand lease history, contact information for the landlord to speak with them.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: to really get a sense of what is the corporate history here?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Is the sale that supposedly occurred at this location from the first LLC to the next, is it legitimate?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Do they have proof of payment for that sale?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Was it contracted?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Or is this just a sham transaction to avoid our sealing authority?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And we'll take a close look at that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And there are times where we will refuse to unseal or move forward with the sealing, even if we have identified that there is a quote-unquote new business operating.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so that tool can be effective, but it is obviously resource intensive.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And that's always going to be true.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We're always happy to target those resources because, of course, this is an important issue.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: But those are some of the issues that we face, I think, with these corporate.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how often DCWP analyzes whether LLC ownership changed. Schwenk says it is a present issue in all sealings and a critical part of the sealing process, and will apply to e-cigarette retailers under the new bill.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks frequency of LLC analysis; Schwenk says present in all sealings

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And how, just jumping to the LLC point for a minute and before, I have a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to you, Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How frequently is that analysis happening, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Where, you know, from the ceiling standpoint, from new LLC to an old LLC, how frequently are you all engaged in?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Are there other agencies that are part of it too?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's a very common practice, but how often are you guys able to really look at that?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, I think that it is a present issue in all of our ceilings.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: So I think, you know, we have targeted, we have sealed 240 TRD businesses since 2023.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We have certainly targeted far more than that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That only reflects the businesses that actually resulted in a ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I think any time we target a ceiling, it is a possibility that we're going to need to dig in on that corporate history.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so it's always present for my team.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: It's something we're always looking at.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I think it is a critical part of the sealing process and will be under, hopefully, this bill once it passes and targeting for electronic cigarette retail dealers as well.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether there is a way to collect fines from a closed LLC that transfers to a new one. Schwenk says there is no formal legal path, but DCWP still sends collection notices and works with the Law Department even after a new LLC appears.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about fine collection when LLC closes; Schwenk says no formal path but efforts continue

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So that's helpful to hear.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So my follow-up question then is I know it sounds like in the sealing context you all are doing the analysis of.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Has the LLC ownership changed?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What's the deliberate evasion, which we know often it is too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But what about right now when it comes to fine collection, right?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So ceiling power will pass legislation.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That'll be helpful there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But for fines, I'm just trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The old LLC, you know, close it down.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: They have an outstanding judgment.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There's no vehicle now to see how the money could transfer from the old LLC to the new one?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think, you know, the first point there is I don't think that there's a formal path in law right now to try to get at that issue of a business that has received past violations.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Senator Cruz, I think you're lost.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This is the city council hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So nice to see you, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You proud of him, but not me?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And then I think the second part there is,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Even if we do think or find out based on a subsequent inspection that the previous LLC has moved on, closed up, we still do engage in collection efforts.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We still are sending out collection notices.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We still are trying to collect on those unpaid penalties, and we still are working with law department and the collections process there.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: As discussed, there are limitations to that, but it's not as if we throw in the towel once we learn of a new LLC.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: So the effort continues.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether the low collection rate reflects few collection actions or difficulty collecting. Ortiz says DCWP tries but many businesses intentionally never intend to comply, and Schwenk adds that frequent inspections can generate large penalties against fly-by-night corporations that never pay.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks to explain 0.5% collection rate; Ortiz and Schwenk cite intentional noncompliance

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So how do you explain the 0.5%?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Is that a, in other words, are there a lot of actions, enforcement actions, or fine collection actions taken, and the 0.5% reflects the difficulty and the inability to collect those fines, or we're very

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: few collections actions actually brought.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand, you know, it's a very low rate, and obviously we'll work together to fix that, but I'm trying to understand, is it a lack of fine collection actions, or is it that the collection rate on those actions is a very low percentage?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Like, you're trying a lot harder, but you're only collecting a few.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it's the latter, where the collection rate is low, but we're trying.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I mean, we engage in a process internally to collect those monies, and then at a certain point, we also refer to a lot of department when there's difficulty that requires their input, too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think the issue here is businesses that I think intentionally are never intending to comply with their obligations in the city.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And they need to be held accountable in different ways than perhaps our typical honest businesses in the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And there are implications on blocking down their location, blocking down the product inside that location.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's also an implication, too, on landlords.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And landlords that harbor recidivist actors also need to be brought into the fold, too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think these businesses, when they're unlicensed like this, particularly in a category that is capped, let's be clear, these two categories are capped.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We're not trying to, the city, based on council law, is not trying to increase the amount of e-cigarette retail dealers or tobacco retailers that are available.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We're not.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's intentionally triting.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Because so any unlicensed actor knows that they're violating the law.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's no way for them to get a license typically.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And so I think it's really about recognizing that these folks don't want to comply, and that's why they need to be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's 100%.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Right, Carlos.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I also do want to add, I think it's important to recognize

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: the relationship between sort of the diligence of our enforcement

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: efforts and what that means for collections.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, in the case of an unlicensed shop that receives violations, we may inspect that location four times in a year.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That may result in four, sometimes eight, oath decisions, four for electronic cigarette violations, four for tobacco violations.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That can result in, over the course of a year, hundreds of thousands of dollars in penalties.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And if this is a fly-by-night corp, have no intention of paying, have every intention of closing up shop once

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: the hammer comes down, either through our sealing authority or through some other effort, then what that means is our sort of diligence and organization in ensuring those inspections take place will reduce our overall collections rate as well.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I don't think that's necessarily a harmful thing, but also doesn't mean that we're not focused on that collections effort.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: But I do think those two things do affect each other.

chapters.summary: Krishnan suggests more aggressive fine collection, possibly with Corp Counsel, as an intermediate step alongside sealing. Ortiz agrees and says DCWP would like to work with the Council on the issue.
chapters.title: Krishnan suggests aggressive fine collection with Corp Counsel; Ortiz agrees

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Well, I do wonder if there are ways that we can all work together to think about and combine collection.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And it's not just with DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In the housing context, too, and we're going to have another oversight hearing on this later in the year, HPD has numerous uncollected violations.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So, you know, I do wonder as you all think about sealing, and that's absolutely important too, but if there's an intermediate

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: a step here of more aggressive fine collection and maybe even working with Corp Council to set up some sort of collection effort could be worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think I agree.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We would love to work on this issue with you as well.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Three violations or three adjudicated by oath summonses?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Adjudicated by oath summonses.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The code, even in the context of this new e-cigarette sealing law,

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: allows or requires a notice of opportunity to be heard for the business.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

chapters.summary: Epstein says the process lets illegal shops operate for years and flip to new LLCs with impunity. Ortiz defends DCWP inspectors' work and suggests the Council consider incorporating SLA-like authority or involving the Sheriff's Office.
chapters.title: Epstein criticizes impunity and LLC flipping; Ortiz defends inspectors and suggests SLA authority

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, think about it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, just think about a regular New Yorker, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So, you know, we walk the street.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I'm going to say this is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And a year goes by, and still the same thing happens.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Two years goes by, same thing happens.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Then you finally issue a sealing order because three times they seal and it's flipped to a new LLC or.

utterances.text: The second time that there's a violation issue, they flip it to an LLC.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Are you starting all over again with a new LLC in the same location, same principles?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Same principles, unless, of course, as Andy was describing earlier, his team's ability to be able to identify if it's actually the same ownership, even though it's a different LLC.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think, I mean, the tension here that you're describing, Chair, is just a due process concern on the business side.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think, you know, we live in these communities, too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We have children in these communities as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I recognize that by myself personally that there's a tension here because we want to remove these places.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: At the same time, then you have an honest business that might say, I want an opportunity to be heard and I need that scheduled in a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I need that rescheduled because something happened to me.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Give me a second chance or a third chance.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Like, that's the other side of the coin.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I agree, like, there are times when, as I said earlier, there are personally, I think, some of these actors are intentionally trying to avoid the law.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But, you know, under the black and white text of the code, they do have certain protections.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm not denying people have protections, but...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If someone was opened up a store to do anything else that was illegal, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It was illegal.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There would be some ability, I would think, to have some kind of powers to do something quicker.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, the idea that it's an illegal vape store selling illegal vapes that are flavored.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You now have issued three summonses.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, they are being adjudicated by oath.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: A year and a half goes by, and the public doesn't see any change.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That sends the wrong message not just to the public, but the people who are going to engage in illegal behavior.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because what they think is, well...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: As long as we just keep doing this and, you know, every two years flip it to a new LLC, there's really nothing that could ever happen.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We could continue to do this operation for year over year over year because of the way the city structured this.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what we've seen is through this report is.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's impunity.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, you're not paying, they're not paying fines because they have no licenses, and they're not being shut down.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And using this LLC loophole could continue to still flip it to a new landlord, to a new entity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I am, I want to just, one thing I want to take a step back.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I do believe, and while there's always room for improvement, that our team is doing a lot of good work out there as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I just want to credit the inspectors, and they deal with incredibly difficult situations too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: These unlicensed actors, I want to get this in, because these unlicensed actors, for example, they're breaking the laws in many different ways.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And so I just want to make sure that we're not losing sight of the work.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There is a substantial amount of work that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's always room for improvement, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think if there's SLA, I would be interested to see maybe if the council wants to incorporate whatever SLA has the ability to do in this space into this legislation being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
