utterances.text: We created further transparency, especially in the context of landlords.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know it was a big issue that I know Councilmember Krishnan and I have dealt with over the years.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Decades, sorry, to age you there.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But so that law makes that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Now, it doesn't require it to be public, which is a part that, you know, we fought with the governor about back in the day.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But they have it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So do we just need to ask them to give it to you?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think that this is something we could look at more, but I do not think that we have access to that information.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If you could look into and get back to us, I'd like to know where the barriers are here on the LLC front, because

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: since we know some government agency has it, and it sounds like you don't have easy access to it, there is probably a database somewhere at a state agency that could be made available.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We've done this before with HCR and HPD when we wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There was an agreement between HCR and HPD that they would share data, and that probably happened 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So HPD could have that HCR data.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I don't know why we wouldn't be able to get this through some process that we could work out with our state partners.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's certainly something we're more than happy to talk about.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks what tools DCWP has against landlords who lease to illegal vape shops. Schwenk says DCWP contacts landlords during sealing, sends notices, and has found good receptivity from property owners about their obligation not to lease to violating businesses.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about tools against landlords; Schwenk explains sealing notices and landlord engagement

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I think that LLC transparency is important.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But then the question really is, well, you know this is happening because there's a lease for a space that's, you know, use Linda again.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Linda gets a 10-year lease for this space, and then three years in with the violation, she flips it to a new entity.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: She still had a 10-year lease, but now it's flipped to a new entity.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We know the landlord's being complicit in this behavior.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What tools do you have in your tool belt to go after the landlords who we know are being involved in all these illegal sales and products?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, it's an important point, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, as a part of our sealing process, we do engage with the landlords.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We send notices and get...

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: contact with landlords of every location that we do target for a ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And that's been incredibly helpful.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We have found pretty good receptivity from property owners and landlords on many locations.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And they can engage with us both to provide proof of lease history and ownership issues when necessary, and also to

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: really take serious their obligation under the administrative code to not lease or rent their properties to businesses that are violating the law.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether DCWP fines landlords. Schwenk says DCWP filed a large lawsuit in 2025 against a Harlem property owner and corporate tenants with a long history of smoke shop violations, and litigation is ongoing.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about fines against landlords; Schwenk cites Harlem lawsuit

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And do you issue them fines when they continue to engage in this?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Behavior of renting out to business or engaging in illegal behavior?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We, in fact, in 2025, filed a pretty large lawsuit against a property owner in Harlem of a very bad location, you know, long history of smoke shop violations over many corporate tenants.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Filed a lawsuit against both the corporate entities and the landlord and property owner of that location and have been in litigation since, and we hope to resolve it very soon on favorable terms.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And how many times have you used that authority to go against landlords?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, it's incredibly labor-intensive and resource-intensive.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We have used it in a couple different contexts, you know, over the past decade.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think what we have found more effective is engaging directly, you know, getting in contact.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: telling landlords, you have a responsibility here.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think across property owners in the city, I don't think most are aware that they have an obligation to really know what their tenants are doing and to make sure their tenants aren't engaging in unlicensed activity.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That exists in our code, and that's something that we're constantly speaking to landlords about.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Just to reiterate as well, sorry, Chair, to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That at any time we engage in a sealing process, we are contacting the landlord as well.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about notice requirements and how often landlords are fined. Schwenk says DCWP sends sealing notices to landlords, pulls ownership data from city databases, and does deeper research when property LLCs have poor contact information.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about landlord notice process and fines; Schwenk explains property LLC research

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What is the process you use?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, what are the notice requirements?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What are the documents you send over to the landlords when you know this is ongoing?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, are you just sending them a letter?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Are you setting up meetings?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, are you issuing fines?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How often do you issue fines for these landlords?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, as part of the sealing process, you know, when we notice a location for sealing, we will send out a notice to the landlord.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We, you know, we pull that information from, of course, city databases, you know, maintained by DOF and others to identify those property owners.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And when we identify, you know, repeat noncompliance issues, we will do a deeper dive on the landlord itself.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, what we find is that, you know, similar to sometimes the retail LLCs, there are property ownership LLCs that have been, you know,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: LLC opened for the sole purpose of owning and maintaining a single property in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Sometimes that contact information on various databases is.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so we'll do deeper research to try to find individuals or other corporations connected to or associated with that property owner to get in touch and get a response and get that engagement.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I think that's been incredibly helpful.

chapters.summary: Schwenk describes a repeat smoke shop on Willoughby Street in downtown Brooklyn where sealing and Sheriff involvement failed until DCWP engaged the landlord. The landlord filed a corporate holdover proceeding, and the smoke shop was finally shut down.
chapters.title: Schwenk gives downtown Brooklyn smoke shop example

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Like, I would love to share one example in downtown Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We had a longtime repeat smoke shop operating on Willoughby Street.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We had tried sealing, had new corporate entities.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Sheriff was involved, couldn't get any traction.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We finally got engagement from the landlord, worked with the landlord both on the sealing process as well as a corporate holdover proceeding that the landlord was willing to file because of this repeat noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And after working, you know, sort of collaboratively in the end, because of that engagement with the landlord,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Finally got the smoke shop shut down, and there's a dollar slice joint open there now.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so that's the type of, you know, ultimate goal and response we want to see from this engagement.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many fines DCWP has issued against landlords since 2023. Schwenk says he does not think DCWP has that data, and Epstein says he would like to know.
chapters.title: Epstein asks how many landlord fines since 2023; Schwenk says no data

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And since 2023, how many fines have you issued against landlords for this kind of behavior?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't think we have data on that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, we'd love to know that is.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because I do think your point is right, that one is the LLC transparency.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We need to make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Two, maybe there are additional tools we need to have you have to go against these landlords.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And three, I think we need to figure out more ways to have...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Power not to have to wait to three times and sometimes these emergencies especially around schools to be able to to shut down illegal operations like the

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: SLA is able to shut down illegal operations for illegal stores.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I think this is, you know, this report has really highlighted kind of how widespread this problem is.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then we need to make sure we have additional tools.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I want to hand it back to Chair Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know he had additional questions.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks what city law changes could help DCWP enforce against LLCs. Schwenk says the sealing bill is an important first step and DCWP is open to other creative solutions.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks what city law tools DCWP needs for LLC enforcement; Schwenk says sealing bill is first step

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I think this is a really important conversation because I think that that is where a lot of these issues are coming from, is around the LLC, the gap here in enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So one, we were talking about this a bit now with landlords, but what are, besides the changes in state law, which I think would help, but that will take more time, what are...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Things you could see, what things are there in city law that you need or we could work on to give you all more enforcement around these LLCs at the city level?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's a great question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think that the bill in front of us today is an important step.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I think that will help the sealing effort and enforcement effort sort of across the board.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I think if there are other creative solutions either identified by

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: council's team or internally DCWP, we are always happy to raise those.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that we have another ledge proposal on this exact topic to probably share or discuss right now, but moving forward on VAPE LLC, excuse me, VAPE Sealing Authority, I think would be a great first step.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether public health tools could help enforcement. Schwenk says DCWP and DOHMH are concerned about the proliferation of tobacco and vape vending machines and would like to work on a proposal to prohibit them.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about health code tools; Schwenk discusses vending machine prohibition

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Yeah, and then I think keep us posted on that too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I also do wonder, are there any things in the health codes or anything?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, that may, I know the other agencies might get involved there too, DOHMA and otherwise, but are there other public health related tools you could use or enforcement powers you might be able to tie in here, even though it's,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: you know, technically a different set of laws that, you know, it's not totally within your jurisdiction, but I do wonder if there's some coordinated effort there around public health.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I think maybe one public health-related topic that's come up recently and we have discussed somewhat extensively with our colleagues at DOHMH is the sort of, I think,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: upstart proliferation of vending machines for tobacco and vapes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, of course, this was something that I think existed in some of our childhoods, but has come back a bit.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And there are now at least one licensed tobacco vending machine in the city.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think we would love to work on a proposal to prohibit those.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, I don't think that we view that as a good way for retail transactions to be occurring.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think it both presents harm for youth, but at the same time also presents harm for legitimate small businesses in New York City who want to hold these licenses, which are capped and not always available,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: want to hold them in good standing and follow the laws and really run a small business that can be a part of commercial districts.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: So that is something I think, you know, on the public health front could be a helpful topic to discuss.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP has observed clear vapes and flavors in the field and is working with the Health Department on guidance to issue summonses. He says partnership with DOHMH is key.
chapters.title: Ortiz adds clear vape guidance with DOHMH

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And also, I don't know, Chair, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You know, we were observing as well in the field this issue with the clear vapes and flavors.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think especially after meeting with your team, we were able to talk to the health department.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think they're going to be working on guidance that we can use to issue summonses around this issue too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: To your point earlier, I think the partnership is key with the health department to make sure that we are armed with the information we need to issue those summonses.

chapters.summary: Krishnan notes illegal advertising near schools and asks if DCWP can bring advertising claims. Schwenk says DCWP enforces a state law prohibiting display of paraphernalia or advertisements within 500 feet of a school and urges the public to submit complaints identifying the school.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about advertising enforcement; Schwenk explains 500-foot school display law

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And also, what about, and this, I think, falls more within your guys'agency directly, is around advertising.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Like, if there's some sort of deceptive advertising or false advertising,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because our report also found that there is...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: A lot of illegal advertising happening by schools about vapes, both from licensed and unlicensed shops.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And there may be something there, too, because the licensed shops are also marketing illegal vapes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The unlicensed ones shouldn't be doing business at all.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Are there claims you all can bring in the advertising context also that could generate fines that you could also collect on that may, I mean, I don't know if it'll get around the LLC issue, but I just wonder if there's a separate set of

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: laws there that could be helpful too, because there is a big problem of advertising as well.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that the advertising and sort of product display issue is certainly forefront.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think it was a great call out by the council report here.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: There is a state law that we do enforce on displaying paraphernalia or advertisements for these products in the front of shops within 500 feet of a school.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so I would love to call out.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: To everybody, please submit complaints on that issue and identify the school.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That helps us immensely to try to target these inspections and be able to really properly do the measurement and prove up that violation.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That information is also available on our website.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: It is a violation we are checking for and we'll measure for.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And so we're always happy to take in those complaints and target those inspections.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says the report will lead DCWP to reprioritize locations using the data. Krishnan urges DCWP to find creative enforcement and collection tools while state law changes take time.
chapters.title: Ortiz says DCWP will reprioritize locations; Krishnan urges creative tools

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And as I mentioned earlier, too, I think because of this report, we're going to be reprioritizing these locations as well using the data that we received.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Because I think we want to make sure that when we have information like this that we're able to action on it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think this would urge you all to, as you're reprioritizing it, the change at the state level may take more time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But perhaps there are tools and creative ways now to address some of these things and to collect on it, you know, that may work around, maybe some workarounds around the LLC.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: issue as well.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how DCWP inspectors respond to clear vapes. Ortiz says inspectors use a standard checklist, make assessments about whether products fall into the flavor category, and DOHMH is testing products to identify flavors.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks how inspectors handle clear vapes; Ortiz explains checklist and DOHMH testing

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I want to turn it over to clear vapes as well because that's come out.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's a big gray area, although not so gray.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, some of these businesses are saying they're clear and they either they are not they are flavored vapes or they're saying the word clear.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But they are actually, like, meaning the first kind are vapes that are, you know, market is clear, but they have a flavor to them, so they should not be classified as clear.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The other way clear is used, as the report has found, is to actually hide the fact that they are truly illegal flavored vapes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So how are, when your investigators go out to retailers and you come across clear vapes, how are you all reacting in those situations?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What does the inspection look like around clear vapes when that comes up, and how are you all thinking about it now in light of this report?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think typically, Councilman, when we go into a place to inspect them for tobacco or e-cigarette activity, we have a set checklist of what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And it's applicable to everybody.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's no inequitable enforcement, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And the inspector will go down a list of what's happening here and what can I issue summons for.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And they'll identify products, for example, undercover purchases or through their own observations that are violating the law, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And they'll look at the markings and they'll compare.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think clear, I think they're making an assessment as well if that falls into the flavor category.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But I know that as well, after speaking with your team, that the Department of Health is also conducting testing on these products as well to identify the flavors, and we can use that subsequently in our inspections.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to add anything on that.

chapters.summary: Schwenk says the report correctly identifies clear vapes as the latest flavored vape marketing trend. He describes an inspector who identified the vape "OMG" because the letters were made of oranges, mangoes, and guavas, and says DOHMH is identifying which clear products are prohibited.
chapters.title: Schwenk explains clear vape products, OMG example, and DOHMH testing

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I think that's a really good point there, Carlos.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And, Council Member, I think the oversight report, you know, I think got this issue completely correct.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, Clear is, I think, the latest in this sort of line of flavored vape type products and marketing of products.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, I think an important sort of example of what we've seen here in the past is our inspectors identifying a vape that was called OMG.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: You know, on its face.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Maybe not a problematic name or maybe doesn't necessarily mean it is

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: is a flavor, but our inspectors are incredibly well trained on this subject.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: The inspector in this case, you know, took a close look and realized that the O was in fact made up of small little oranges and the M was made up of small little mangoes and the G was made up of small little guavas and issued a violation for that product.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And then we're able to establish, you know, that going forward, OMG, take a look, you know, and train on that issue.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think clear is, you know, kind of the next step.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: What Carlos said is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We've been working very closely with DOHMH.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: They're very aware of these clear products and are currently undergoing a process to try to identify the particular ones that would fall under the prohibited flavored category and those that don't.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: That will allow us to more easily identify those in the field beyond the upfront steps our inspectors are already taking to identify those.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether DCWP is developing guidance for inspectors on clear vapes. Schwenk says yes, DCWP is incorporating the Council report and DOHMH work into training and will identify common clear products that are flavored.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about guidance to inspectors on clear vapes; Schwenk says yes

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And have you all started thinking about guidance to issue to your inspectors or within the agency about how to think differently about clear vapes now, given all that we're seeing?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We're taking in the council report, you know, working with DOHMH on that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: We are constantly training our inspectors on this issue, among others.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: But we'll certainly be incorporating, you know, particularized guidance on the clear issue.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And, you know, along with that, identifying individual products that are most common and use clear that we do know are flavored.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: And that allows us to not spin our wheels and identify those quickly during an inspection.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how DCWP views clear vapes, suggesting any flavor should make them illegal. Schwenk says that is part of the ongoing process and could inform future conversations with the Council.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks agency position on clear vapes; Schwenk says part of process

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so what is the, as you all are talking about DOHMH now too, what is the agency position?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: or I know it's being formed now, but how are you all thinking about clear vapes in particular?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because it seems to me there's a real case to classify them as illegal if they have any kind of flavor whatsoever, whether it's deliberately, you know,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: retailers are lying about them and saying that they're clear when they're not, or it's considered clear but has a slight flavor to it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So are you all thinking about coming out with some sort of guidance, too, that makes clear when clear vapes are actually illegal products?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Schwenk
utterances.text: I think that's part of the process we're discussing now, and I think also could be helpful for future conversations with council on some potential next steps there.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether inspectors check product labeling accuracy. Schwenk says inspectors do close visual inspections for flavor representations and package size violations, and notes that flavored products enter the country with little federal restriction.
chapters.title: Krishnan asks about product labeling accuracy; Schwenk explains visual inspections and federal import issues

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And when investigators go out now, are they also looking at the accuracy of product labeling?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I mean, obviously, in the clear vape context, that's going to be really important.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But overall, when the investigation is happening and retailers are providing vapes, are you all looking at whether what they're saying matches actually what the product is?

summary: The Committee on Oversight and Investigations, jointly with Consumer and Worker Protection, holds a hearing on flavored e-cigarette availability near NYC schools and Intro 1167, which would grant DCWP authority to seal e-cigarette retailers.

DCWP testifies about enforcement efforts, inspection statistics, collection challenges, LLC evasion, and supports the sealing bill; council members press on school proximity, fines, landlords, and the supply chain.

Public witness David Schwartz of the New York Association of Wholesalers and Distributors describes how the illegal market harms licensed businesses and offers to share intelligence on illegal distributors.
